label: Mycology
blurb: Dimorphic fungi, yeasts, molds — morphology, endemic region, and antifungals

organisms.name: Candida albicans
organisms.labFeatures: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae at 20 C and germ tubes at 37 C; forms a true hypha; germ tube test positive; grows on Sabouraud agar; part of normal flora
organisms.manifestations: Oral thrush, esophagitis in AIDS, vulvovaginitis, diaper dermatitis, intertrigo, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, candidemia and endocarditis in neutropenic or catheterized patients
organisms.treatment: Topical nystatin or clotrimazole for mucosal disease; fluconazole for esophagitis; echinocandin such as caspofungin for candidemia
organisms.transmission: Endogenous overgrowth of normal flora after antibiotics, corticosteroids, diabetes, or immunosuppression; direct inoculation via central lines
organisms.virulenceFactor: Phenotypic switching between yeast and hyphal forms for tissue invasion, adhesins, secreted aspartyl proteases, and biofilm formation on catheters
organisms.tooltip: Esophagitis means CD4 below 100 and is an AIDS-defining illness; thrush alone is not. T-cell defects give mucocutaneous disease, while neutrophil defects give disseminated candidemia.

organisms.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
organisms.labFeatures: Encapsulated yeast with narrow-based budding; India ink or mucicarmine stain shows the capsule; latex agglutination for capsular antigen in CSF; soap-bubble lesions in basal ganglia
organisms.manifestations: Subacute meningoencephalitis with headache and raised intracranial pressure in AIDS with CD4 below 100; pneumonia; cutaneous lesions
organisms.treatment: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine for induction, then fluconazole consolidation and maintenance; serial lumbar punctures for pressure control
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of yeast from soil contaminated with pigeon droppings; no person-to-person spread
organisms.virulenceFactor: Thick polysaccharide capsule blocks phagocytosis and complement; melanin production via laccase; urease aids CNS invasion
organisms.tooltip: Repeated lumbar punctures to relieve pressure matter as much as antifungals for survival. Cryptococcal antigen is more sensitive than India ink. Pigeon droppings are the exposure clue.

organisms.name: Histoplasma capsulatum
organisms.labFeatures: Mold with microconidia and tuberculate macroconidia in soil at 25 C; small intracellular yeast within macrophages at 37 C; urine antigen; granulomas with calcification
organisms.manifestations: Usually asymptomatic or flu-like pulmonary illness; cavitary lung disease; disseminated disease with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and oral ulcers in AIDS; mediastinal fibrosis
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole for mild to moderate disease; liposomal amphotericin B for severe or disseminated disease
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of microconidia from soil enriched with bird or bat droppings — caves, chicken coops, and the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys
organisms.virulenceFactor: Survival and replication inside macrophage phagolysosomes by alkalinizing the compartment and acquiring iron and calcium
organisms.tooltip: Histo Hides (inside macrophages). Mississippi and Ohio River valleys, bat and bird droppings, caves. Disseminated disease in AIDS shows pancytopenia from marrow involvement.

organisms.name: Blastomyces dermatitidis
organisms.labFeatures: Mold at 25 C; broad-based budding yeast with a thick doubly refractile wall at 37 C; KOH prep of skin lesions or sputum; pyogranulomatous inflammation
organisms.manifestations: Acute or chronic pneumonia that can mimic malignancy; verrucous skin lesions with heaped-up borders; osteomyelitis; prostatitis; rarely CNS disease
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole for mild to moderate disease; liposomal amphotericin B for severe disease or CNS involvement
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of conidia from moist decaying wood and soil near rivers in the Great Lakes, Ohio, and Mississippi River basins
organisms.virulenceFactor: BAD1 adhesin promotes macrophage binding and suppresses TNF; thick yeast cell wall resists killing
organisms.tooltip: Blastomyces Buds Broadly. Great Lakes and Ohio River valley, rotting wood. Verrucous skin lesions that look like squamous cell carcinoma are the classic extrapulmonary finding.

organisms.name: Coccidioides immitis
organisms.labFeatures: Mold with barrel-shaped arthroconidia in soil; large spherules packed with endospores in tissue at 37 C; eosinophilia common; serology or antigen testing
organisms.manifestations: Valley fever with pneumonia, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias (desert rheumatism); cavitary lung disease; disseminated infection to meninges, bone, and skin
organisms.treatment: Fluconazole or itraconazole; lifelong fluconazole for coccidioidal meningitis; amphotericin B for severe disseminated disease
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of arthroconidia from dust in the southwestern United States and Central Valley of California; risk rises after earthquakes and dust storms
organisms.virulenceFactor: Spherules too large for phagocytosis that rupture to release hundreds of endospores; arthroconidia are highly infectious at low dose
organisms.tooltip: Spherules, not budding yeast — the one dimorphic fungus whose tissue form is not a yeast. Southwest dust exposure plus erythema nodosum plus eosinophilia is the classic triad.

organisms.name: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
organisms.labFeatures: Mold at 25 C; yeast with multiple buds in a captain's wheel or mariner's wheel arrangement at 37 C; KOH or silver stain of tissue
organisms.manifestations: Chronic pulmonary disease, painful oral and nasal mucosal ulcers, cervical lymphadenopathy, and skin lesions; predominantly affects adult men
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole for most cases, often prolonged; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as an alternative; amphotericin B for severe disease
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of conidia from soil in rural Latin America, especially Brazil; agricultural workers are at highest risk
organisms.virulenceFactor: Estrogen inhibits the mold-to-yeast transition, which explains the striking male predominance; gp43 adhesin mediates tissue binding
organisms.tooltip: Captain's wheel morphology — a central yeast with multiple peripheral buds. The male predominance is real and mechanistic: estrogen blocks conversion to the pathogenic yeast form.

organisms.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
organisms.labFeatures: Septate hyphae branching at acute 45-degree angles; conidiophores with radiating conidia; galactomannan antigen; monomorphic mold that does not form yeast
organisms.manifestations: Invasive aspergillosis with angioinvasion and hemoptysis in neutropenia; allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma and cystic fibrosis; aspergilloma in old cavities; aflatoxin-related hepatocellular carcinoma
organisms.treatment: Voriconazole is first-line for invasive disease; isavuconazole or liposomal amphotericin B as alternatives; corticosteroids for allergic bronchopulmonary disease
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of ubiquitous airborne conidia from compost, construction dust, and water-damaged buildings
organisms.virulenceFactor: Angioinvasion causing thrombosis and infarction; gliotoxin suppresses neutrophils; aflatoxin from A. flavus is a potent hepatocarcinogen causing p53 mutation
organisms.tooltip: Septate hyphae at 45 degrees versus Mucor's wide-angle nonseptate hyphae. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is treated with steroids, the opposite of invasive disease.

organisms.name: Mucor and Rhizopus species
organisms.labFeatures: Broad, ribbon-like nonseptate hyphae branching at wide 90-degree angles; rapid growth on culture; biopsy shows angioinvasion with necrosis
organisms.manifestations: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis with black necrotic eschar on the palate or nasal turbinates, proptosis, and cranial neuropathies in diabetic ketoacidosis; pulmonary and cutaneous forms
organisms.treatment: Urgent surgical debridement plus liposomal amphotericin B; posaconazole or isavuconazole for step-down; correct the underlying acidosis or neutropenia
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of spores from soil and decaying organic matter, or direct inoculation through burns and wounds
organisms.virulenceFactor: Ketone reductase allows growth in the high-glucose acidotic environment of DKA; CotH receptors bind endothelium driving angioinvasion and infarction
organisms.tooltip: Diabetic ketoacidosis plus black palatal eschar plus proptosis is a surgical emergency. Ketone reductase explains why DKA specifically predisposes. Nonseptate wide-angle hyphae distinguish it from Aspergillus.

organisms.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
organisms.labFeatures: Disc or cup-shaped cysts on methenamine silver or immunofluorescence of induced sputum or lavage; elevated beta-D-glucan and LDH; cannot be cultured; cholesterol instead of ergosterol in its membrane
organisms.manifestations: Subacute dyspnea with dry cough and hypoxia disproportionate to findings; diffuse bilateral ground-glass interstitial infiltrates; pneumothorax
organisms.treatment: High-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with adjunctive corticosteroids if PaO2 is below 70; TMP-SMX prophylaxis when CD4 is below 200
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of airborne organisms, with most people exposed in childhood; disease reflects reactivation or reinfection under immunosuppression
organisms.virulenceFactor: Tight adherence to type I pneumocytes causing alveolar damage; major surface glycoprotein antigenic variation; cholesterol-based membrane makes it resistant to amphotericin
organisms.tooltip: CD4 below 200 is the threshold for both prophylaxis and disease. Its membrane uses cholesterol rather than ergosterol, which is exactly why amphotericin and azoles do not work on it.

organisms.name: Malassezia furfur
organisms.labFeatures: KOH prep shows spaghetti and meatballs appearance of short hyphae and yeast clusters; lipid-dependent so it requires olive oil overlay to culture; yellow-green fluorescence under Wood lamp
organisms.manifestations: Tinea versicolor with hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly macules on the trunk; seborrheic dermatitis and dandruff; catheter-related fungemia in neonates on lipid infusions
organisms.treatment: Topical selenium sulfide, ketoconazole shampoo, or topical azole; oral fluconazole for extensive disease
organisms.transmission: Overgrowth of normal skin flora in hot humid weather, with sweating and oily skin; not contagious
organisms.virulenceFactor: Azelaic acid production inhibits tyrosinase causing the hypopigmentation; lipase degrades sebum triglycerides driving inflammation
organisms.tooltip: The hypopigmentation persists after treatment because azelaic acid has already inhibited melanocyte tyrosinase — tell patients the color takes months to return. Spaghetti and meatballs on KOH.

organisms.name: Sporothrix schenckii
organisms.labFeatures: Mold with rosette-shaped conidia on delicate hyphae at 25 C; cigar-shaped budding yeast in tissue at 37 C; asteroid bodies on histology
organisms.manifestations: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis with an ulcerating nodule at the inoculation site and ascending nodules along lymphatic channels; pulmonary and disseminated forms in the immunocompromised
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole for several months; amphotericin B for disseminated or pulmonary disease; potassium iodide historically
organisms.transmission: Traumatic inoculation from rose thorns, sphagnum moss, hay, and soil — rose gardener's disease; also from cat scratches
organisms.virulenceFactor: Melanin in the cell wall resists oxidative killing; thermotolerance permitting growth at body temperature and lymphatic spread
organisms.tooltip: Gardener pricked by a thorn, then a chain of nodules marching up the arm along lymphatics. Cigar-shaped yeast in tissue. Nodular lymphangitis has a short differential — this leads it.

organisms.name: Trichophyton species
organisms.labFeatures: KOH prep shows branching septate hyphae in skin scrapings; grows on dermatophyte test medium; does not fluoresce (unlike Microsporum)
organisms.manifestations: Tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis with annular scaly plaques and central clearing, tinea unguium (onychomycosis), and tinea capitis with alopecia
organisms.treatment: Topical terbinafine or azole for skin; oral terbinafine or griseofulvin for nail and scalp infection, which topicals cannot penetrate
organisms.transmission: Direct contact with infected skin, contaminated floors, shared towels, and animals; warm moist environments favor it
organisms.virulenceFactor: Keratinases that digest keratin allowing colonization of stratum corneum, nails, and hair while remaining superficial
organisms.tooltip: Dermatophytes stay in keratinized tissue and never invade living tissue. Scalp and nail disease requires oral therapy because topicals cannot reach the hair follicle or nail matrix.

organisms.name: Microsporum canis
organisms.labFeatures: KOH prep shows septate hyphae; spindle-shaped macroconidia on culture; blue-green fluorescence of infected hairs under Wood lamp
organisms.manifestations: Tinea capitis in children with scaly patches and broken hairs; tinea corporis; kerion as a boggy inflammatory mass
organisms.treatment: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for tinea capitis; selenium sulfide shampoo to reduce spore shedding; treat infected pets
organisms.transmission: Contact with infected cats and dogs, and person-to-person among children sharing hats or combs
organisms.virulenceFactor: Keratinase-mediated invasion of hair shafts (ectothrix pattern) causing hair breakage and inflammatory response
organisms.tooltip: The dermatophyte that fluoresces under Wood lamp, unlike Trichophyton. A child with tinea capitis and a new kitten points here, and the pet needs treatment too.

organisms.name: Epidermophyton floccosum
organisms.labFeatures: KOH prep with septate hyphae; club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and no microconidia on culture; does not invade hair
organisms.manifestations: Tinea cruris (jock itch) and tinea pedis; onychomycosis; notably spares the hair and scalp
organisms.treatment: Topical terbinafine, clotrimazole, or miconazole; keep the area dry
organisms.transmission: Person-to-person contact, shared locker room floors, and contaminated clothing and towels
organisms.virulenceFactor: Keratinase activity restricted to skin and nails, with inability to invade hair follicles
organisms.tooltip: The dermatophyte that never infects hair, which distinguishes it from Trichophyton and Microsporum. Produces macroconidia but no microconidia on culture.

organisms.name: Candida auris
organisms.labFeatures: Budding yeast that does not form pseudohyphae; frequently misidentified by conventional systems so MALDI-TOF or molecular methods are needed; often resistant to fluconazole and sometimes echinocandins
organisms.manifestations: Candidemia, wound and ear infection, and urinary tract infection in ICU patients; high mortality in outbreaks
organisms.treatment: Echinocandin first-line pending susceptibilities; amphotericin B for echinocandin-resistant strains; strict contact precautions
organisms.transmission: Person-to-person and environmental surfaces in healthcare facilities; persistent skin colonization allows silent spread
organisms.virulenceFactor: Thermotolerance and salt tolerance, prolonged survival on dry surfaces, biofilm formation, and intrinsic multidrug resistance
organisms.tooltip: An emerging nosocomial threat notable for multidrug resistance and environmental persistence. Unlike C. albicans it does not form pseudohyphae and is routinely misidentified by older lab systems.

organisms.name: Talaromyces marneffei
organisms.labFeatures: Mold producing a diffusible red pigment at 25 C; yeast with characteristic transverse septa dividing by fission rather than budding at 37 C
organisms.manifestations: Disseminated infection in advanced HIV with fever, weight loss, papular skin lesions with central umbilication, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia
organisms.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B induction followed by itraconazole; secondary prophylaxis until immune reconstitution
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of conidia from soil in Southeast Asia, southern China, and northeastern India; bamboo rats are an associated reservoir
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular survival in macrophages; yeast replication by fission; melanin and catalase-peroxidase resisting oxidative killing
organisms.tooltip: An AIDS-defining illness in Southeast Asia. Umbilicated papules mimic molluscum or cryptococcosis. It is the only dimorphic fungus whose yeast divides by fission, not budding.

organisms.name: Fusarium species
organisms.labFeatures: Septate hyphae with banana or canoe-shaped macroconidia; positive blood cultures (unusual for a mold); angioinvasive on biopsy
organisms.manifestations: Keratitis in contact lens wearers, onychomycosis, and disseminated infection with painful skin nodules in profound neutropenia
organisms.treatment: Voriconazole or liposomal amphotericin B, often combined; recovery of neutrophil count is critical; surgical debridement
organisms.transmission: Environmental soil and plant exposure; contaminated contact lens solution; inhalation or direct inoculation
organisms.virulenceFactor: Angioinvasion with thrombosis, intrinsic resistance to many antifungals, and mycotoxin production
organisms.tooltip: One of the few molds that grows in blood cultures. Keratitis in a contact lens wearer and disseminated disease with skin nodules in a neutropenic patient are the two presentations to know.

organisms.name: Scedosporium apiospermum
organisms.labFeatures: Septate hyphae resembling Aspergillus on histology; distinguished only by culture; intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B
organisms.manifestations: Mycetoma after traumatic inoculation, sinopulmonary colonization in cystic fibrosis, brain abscess after near-drowning, and disseminated disease in transplant recipients
organisms.treatment: Voriconazole is the drug of choice; surgical debridement; amphotericin B is ineffective
organisms.transmission: Traumatic inoculation from soil, and aspiration of polluted water in near-drowning events
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B and many azoles, plus melanized cell wall resisting oxidative killing
organisms.tooltip: Looks exactly like Aspergillus in tissue but is amphotericin resistant — which is why culture identification changes management. Brain abscess after near-drowning is the classic vignette.
